title: Act III, Scene IV

teacherSummary.text: At the state banquet a Murderer tells Macbeth that Banquo is dead but Fleance escaped. When Macbeth wishes Banquo were present, Banquo's ghost sits in his place, seen only by Macbeth, who cries 'Thou canst not say I did it.' Lady Macbeth explains it as a fit he has had since youth and scolds him ('Are you a man?'). The ghost returns; the feast breaks up in disorder. Afterwards Macbeth says 'blood will have blood,' notes that Macduff refused to come, and resolves to visit the Witches: 'I am in blood stepp'd in so far…'

context.history: Elizabethan audiences debated whether ghosts were spirits of the dead or devils in disguise; the play never settles whether this ghost is real.

significance: The banquet, a symbol of social order and kingship, collapses. Macbeth's public breakdown exposes him to the thanes and marks Lady Macbeth's last scene of control.

It will have blood; they say, blood will have blood:
Stones have been known to move and trees to speak;
Augurs and understood relations have
By magot-pies and choughs and rooks brought forth
The secret’st man of blood.

I pray you, speak not; he grows worse and worse;
Question enrages him.

O, these flaws and starts,
Impostors to true fear, would well become
A woman’s story at a winter’s fire,
Authorized by her grandam.

Thou art the best o’ the cut-throats: yet he’s good
That did the like for Fleance: if thou didst it,
Thou art the nonpareil.

You have displaced the mirth, broke the good meeting,
With most admired disorder.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Thou canst not say I did it: never shake / Thy gory locks at me” slowly and put it in my own words: Seeing Banquo's ghost at the feast, Macbeth cries that the ghost cannot say he did it, and tells it not to shake its bloody hair at him. Next, craft. I notice that his denial actually reveals his guilt. The strongest word is “gory”: it describes the ghost's bloody hair, a sign of murder. Then, effect. What does Macbeth say to Banquo's ghost? My answer: Macbeth tells Banquo's ghost that he cannot say Macbeth did it and must not shake his bloody hair at him; his outburst before the lords exposes his guilt and the feast falls apart.
